scout.purpose: Android windows resize across phones, tablets, foldables, split screen, and desktop, requiring state continuity while visible pane structure changes.
scout.realWorldUse: Shopping catalogues, mail, settings, and media browsers benefit from list-detail or supporting-pane layouts and adaptive navigation chrome.
scout.outcome: Use window-adaptive information, preserve selection across panes, and compare adaptive Material scaffolds with explicit Navigation 3 back stacks.

sections.title: Adapt to the current app window

blocks.text: Adaptive decisions use the current application window, not a remembered device category or orientation. Window size classes and posture information describe available space and fold features as they change. Compact layouts may show one destination, while expanded layouts can show related panes together. Adaptation is more than stretching: navigation may switch between bottom bar and rail, lists may gain detail panes, and content width may be bounded for readability. State belongs above these structural branches.

blocks.caption: One selected product key drives single- or multi-pane presentation as the window changes.

sections.title: Canonical panes preserve one state model

blocks.text: List-detail and supporting-pane scaffolds encode canonical behaviour, pane roles, directives, and navigation. A selected product must have one stable identity whether only detail is visible or list and detail appear together. Resizing should not create a second ViewModel, lose scroll position, or push a duplicate destination. Fold hinges and occlusion influence placement in addition to width. Back behaviour depends on the current pane and history, so test compact-to-expanded and expanded-to-compact transitions during a selected detail.

blocks.caption: One selected product key drives single- or multi-pane presentation as the window changes.

blocks.title: Resize is a runtime event
blocks.text: The same destination and state must survive structural changes while the app stays open.

sections.title: Navigation 3 makes back stack data explicit

blocks.text: Established Navigation Compose hides back-stack mechanics behind NavController, while Navigation 3 represents entries as app-owned keys rendered by NavDisplay. Scene strategies may display more than one entry in an adaptive scene. The conceptual lessons are transferable: stable destination keys, minimal arguments, scoped retained state, and explicit back mutation. Choose a navigation generation according to project maturity and requirements, and isolate it behind route callbacks so feature content does not depend on either library.

Production readiness requires evidence beyond a happy-path demonstration. State the owner and lifetime of every mutable value, the expected response to failure or cancellation, and the behaviour after recreation or a second simultaneous request. Exercise long and translated content, large font scale, alternate input, slow dependencies, and rapid repeated actions wherever they apply. Prefer deterministic unit tests for pure logic, integration tests at library and protocol boundaries, and device tests when platform lifecycle, rendering, accessibility, or system UI is part of the contract. Do not hide a missing decision behind a generic helper. A future engineer should be able to identify what may run concurrently, what survives, what is authoritative, and which evidence proves the implementation remains correct.

steps.label: Define contract
steps.detail: Name ownership, lifetime, inputs, outputs, failure, and cancellation.

steps.label: Implement
steps.detail: Choose the smallest API that preserves those semantics.

steps.label: Exercise boundaries
steps.detail: Test absence, failure, recreation, concurrency, and unusual input.

steps.label: Collect evidence
steps.detail: Use semantics, deterministic tests, traces, or protocol inspection.

steps.label: Harden
steps.detail: Fix the demonstrated risk and document the remaining trade-off.

inspect.title: Remove device-name branching
walkthrough: Hardware name does not describe the current app window or split-screen bounds.
The same device can move between compact and expanded space at runtime.
Derive structure from current adaptive window information and keep shared state above it.
inspect.expectedOutput: Resizing changes pane structure without resetting the selected product.

trap_check.mistake: Creating independent selection state inside list and detail branches.
trap_check.why: Resize or navigation can show divergent product identities.
trap_check.fix: Hoist one stable selection or back-stack key above adaptive presentation.

trap_check.mistake: Adding abstraction or optimisation before defining the failure.
trap_check.why: The code becomes harder while ownership, correctness, or measured cost remains unresolved.
trap_check.fix: First write a boundary test or collect evidence that identifies the real defect.

challenge_intro.task: Create compact and expanded product navigation with list-detail panes, retained selection, predictive back expectations, and a documented Navigation Compose versus Navigation 3 boundary.
challenge_intro.successLooksLike: Selection and scroll state survive live resize. Compact and expanded back behaviour is tested. Feature content has no dependency on a navigation controller.

recall.answer: Stable destination, selection, and screen state.
An application-owned list of back-stack keys.

objectives: Preserve state through resize and posture.
